hint_ladder.title: Orient
hint_ladder.text: This word is all about fairness. Think of the word 'equity' — it's a term you might hear in law or business, and it always points to balance and justice.

hint_ladder.title: Rule
hint_ladder.text: When you see 'equitable,' remember the root 'equal.' Anything equitable treats people the same way, without playing favorites.

hint_ladder.title: Apply
hint_ladder.text: Now look at the options. Which one describes treating everyone the same, without bias or unfairness? That's your match.

hint_ladder.title: Nearly There
hint_ladder.text: The answer is the one that means 'fair and just.' The other three all describe the opposite — unfairness, prejudice, or randomness.

A.text: It's easy to see 'unfair' and think it might be related, but it's actually the exact opposite. 'Equitable' means fair, so 'unfair' is a trap for anyone rushing through the options.

B.text: If someone is biased, they're showing favoritism — the opposite of being equitable. This is another antonym trap that catches test-takers who don't pause to check the meaning.

C.text: Correct. 'Equitable' comes from 'equity,' which is all about fairness and justice. When something is equitable, it treats everyone the same way, without bias or unfairness.

D.text: 'Arbitrary' means based on random choice or whim, not on any rule of fairness. It's the opposite of equitable, which is grounded in justice and impartiality.

next_time_rule: When you see 'equitable,' think 'equal treatment.' If an option suggests unfairness, bias, or randomness, it's the wrong path. Your mental shortcut: 'Equitable = Equal + Fair.'
deconstruct_text: Let's break this down simply. The word 'equitable' comes from 'equity,' which is all about fairness and justice. Imagine a judge in court — they're supposed to be equitable, meaning they treat everyone the same, without bias. Now look at the options. 'Unfair' and 'biased' are clearly the opposite — they describe situations where someone is not treating people equally. 'Arbitrary' is a bit trickier; it means something is decided randomly, without any principle of fairness. That leaves 'fair and just,' which directly matches the meaning of equitable. Here's a mental trick to lock this in: whenever you see 'equitable,' think of the word 'equal.' Both share the idea of balance and impartiality. If an option suggests the opposite — unfairness, prejudice, or randomness — you know it's a trap.
